patches/img: A language model reads one vector per token. To show it a picture, make the picture vectors too. Take an image of three thirty six by three thirty six pixels.
patches/count: Cut it into patches of fourteen pixels: three thirty six over fourteen is twenty four per side, and twenty four times twenty four is five hundred and seventy six patches.
patches/vit: A vision transformer, already trained, turns each patch into a vector, here of one thousand and twenty four numbers.
patches/drop: Keep only the patch vectors, all five hundred and seventy six, and leave out the class token.
project/width: The language model has its own width, d: here four thousand and ninety six. Its word vectors are that long, and the patch vectors are not.
project/W: So a projection maps each one across: a learned matrix, W, of one thousand and twenty four by four thousand and ninety six, plus a bias.
project/count: Every patch shares it: one thousand and twenty four times four thousand and ninety six weights, plus four thousand and ninety six biases. About four point two million parameters.
project/mlp: Some models use a small MLP instead, two maps with an activation between, counted like any MLP.
project/prompt: The projected vectors are the image tokens. They go into the prompt first, and the text's embeddings follow.
project/read: From there it is a plain decoder-only model. Each text token attends back to every image token, and the reply comes one token at a time.
train/s1: Training comes in two stages. In stage one, both models are frozen, and only the projection learns, on images paired with captions.
train/loss: The language model must predict each caption from the image tokens, with the usual cross-entropy. Only W can move, so it learns to make vectors the language model already understands.
train/s2: In stage two, the language model trains with the projection, on instructions: an image, a question, and a good answer. The vision transformer stays frozen.
try/window: Image tokens take room. If the model reads at most T max tokens, say twenty forty eight, this image leaves fourteen seventy two for text.
try/p1: Try one. A two twenty four by two twenty four image comes in fourteen pixel patches. How many image tokens does it give?
try/a1: Two twenty four over fourteen is sixteen per side, and sixteen times sixteen is two hundred and fifty six.
try/a2: With twenty forty eight at most, that leaves seventeen ninety two tokens for text.
